title: American Magic buys Danish SailGP team for $60m
content:
Editor’s note: This story is part of The Athletic’s coverage of SailGP, an international sailing competition that has been likened to Formula 1 on water. Follow SailGP here.

U.S. businessman Doug DeVos and his American Magic sailing management group have bought the Danish SailGP team, Rockwool Racing, for $60 million.

After mounting two campaigns for the 2021 and 2024 editions of the America’s Cup, DeVos has now pivoted his competitive attention and investment capital towards SailGP.

Sports team ownership and management is familiar territory — the DeVos family has owned the NBA’s Orlando Magic since 1991.

“We’ve been in touch with SailGP for a long, long time,” DeVos told The Athletic. “Going back to the America’s Cup in Auckland in 2021, we were connecting with Russell (Sir Russell Coutts, CEO of SailGP), hearing from him what was happening, and at the time we were all coming out of COVID, everyone kind of finding the path forward.”

As to the connection with Danish skipper Nicolai Sehested, he said: “We’ve had a relationship with Nicolai; he’s sailed with us on our TP52 Windquest on the Great Lakes. One thing led to another and we just kept the conversation going.”

According to American Magic CEO Mike Cazer: “American Magic purchased 100 percent of the team’s equity, to the value of $60 million. It reflects a combination of the ascendancy of SailGP, all of the momentum it has, and frankly also the partnership with Rockwool and its commitment to the team; it gave us great confidence in acquiring the team for that valuation.”

Andrew Thompson, SailGP’s managing director, pointed towards the dramatic breakage of the Australian team’s wingmast in San Francisco last March as a catalyst in developing the relationship and discussions between American Magic and the league.

“We’ve been familiar with Doug and Terry (Hutchinson, former America’s Cup skipper and American Magic’s president of sailing operations) and Mike for many years,” he told The Athletic. “What moved this forward considerably was last year, when we had the wing failure on the boats in San Francisco.

“Our ship was on the way to Rio, and we had to divert the ship and get the wings fixed in time for our New York race. It just so happened that Pensacola, Florida, had an up-and-coming performance centre and boatbuilding facility that meant we were able to work with the American Magic team. They provided labour and lots of support for us to get the circuit back in action then. So really, we’ve developed the relationship from there.”

Rockwool, headquartered in Copenhagen and one of the world’s biggest manufacturers of stone wool insulation, initially got involved in SailGP’s first season in 2019. But that soon morphed into the company managing the overall operation.

Rockwool’s senior vice president, Mirella Vitale, explained that its responsibilities have grown to the point where it needs help to take the sports team forward. “We became so passionate about SailGP and the project that at a certain point we ended up operating the team as well as sponsoring the team,” she said. “Probably a little bit of craziness behind that, but something that we needed to do in order to ensure that we had a Danish team on the water. And it was important for Rockwool to be part of that Danish sailing history.”

Mirella said Rockwool would continue to be the title sponsor of the team with a commitment through to 2032. So why the sale to American Magic? “We feel that American Magic will complement us. We’ll continue to do what we know how to do.

“But what we were missing was professionalizing the team and actually managing a sports team. I think we have the best partner we could possibly wish for in American Magic.”

As to the possible Americanization of Sehested’s existing group of sailors, Hutchinson told The Athletic: “We’re very focused on the Danish portion of our team and the existing sailors that are with us.” He emphasized that there was more than enough to think about with the coming weekend of grand prix competition in Auckland. “It’s a very talented group of sailors, and to look much past the next three days, I think, would be a mistake.”

With a forecast of strong winds on an extremely tight race area in Auckland Harbor this Saturday and Sunday, the new working partnership between the Danish sailors and their American owners will soon be put to the toughest of tests.
